CASE 04 · HIP FRACTURE

Left hip fracture: reading the X-ray and planning recovery

A break through the trochanteric region of the left hip, explained from the X-ray, with the treatment approach and a week-by-week healing plan.

  • Area: Left hip
  • Fracture: Intertrochanteric
  • Bone healing: 12–16 weeks
Read the case ↓

Hip fractures are among the most important injuries in older adults. They often follow a simple fall at home, especially when bones are weakened by osteoporosis. Prompt surgery and early walking make a major difference to recovery and safety.

Condition
Intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur
Usual treatment
Surgical fixation with a hip nail or screw
Standing
Usually within 1–2 days of surgery
Hospital stay
Usually 4–7 days
Bone healing
About 12–16 weeks
Final result
6–12 months

Tap or click an image to view it full size.

01

What the X-ray shows

This is a front view of the whole pelvis. The side marked “RT” is the patient’s right; the normal right hip gives a useful comparison:

  • A fracture between the two trochanters: in the left hip, a fracture line runs diagonally from the greater trochanter (the bony prominence on the outer side of the hip) towards the lesser trochanter (the smaller bump on the inner side). This is called an intertrochanteric fracture.
  • A separate inner fragment: the bone around the lesser trochanter has broken away as a separate piece. Loss of this inner support makes the fracture less stable, so it needs firm fixation.
  • Ball still in the socket: the femoral head (ball) remains seated in the hip socket. The hip joint itself is preserved, so the bone can be fixed rather than replaced.
  • Normal right hip: the opposite hip is intact, and comparing both sides helps the surgeon restore the correct leg length and angle.
02

Typical symptoms

After this kind of fracture, people usually cannot stand or put weight on the leg, feel pain in the groin or outer hip, and the leg may look shorter and turned outwards. Any fall followed by inability to bear weight should be assessed the same day.

03

How this fracture is treated

Fractures of this pattern are almost always treated with surgery, ideally within 24–48 hours once the patient is medically optimised. The aim is to make the hip strong enough to stand on straight away.

  • Proximal femoral nail (PFN): a rod placed inside the thigh bone through a small incision, with a screw passing up into the femoral head. It is especially suited to unstable patterns like this one.
  • Sliding hip screw and plate: an option for some more stable fractures.
  • Alignment first: the fracture is aligned on a special traction table under live X-ray before the implant is placed, so the leg length and rotation are restored.

The final choice of implant is made by the surgeon after reviewing the full X-rays and the patient’s bone quality and health.

04

Why early surgery matters

Long bed rest after a hip fracture brings risks such as chest infection, blood clots, pressure sores and loss of muscle strength. Stable fixation lets patients sit out of bed and begin walking within a day or two, which protects their overall health as well as the hip.

Recovery and healing timeline

Every recovery is individual. These are the typical stages, and your own plan will be adjusted at each follow-up visit.

Wound healingAbout 2 weeksStitches or staples removed at 12–14 days
Bone healingAbout 12–16 weeksVisible on follow-up X-rays
Full recoveryAbout 6–12 monthsBone health care continues
  1. Days 1–2

    Sitting and standing

    With the physiotherapy team, patients sit out of bed and stand with a walker. Weight-bearing is guided by the surgeon according to the fixation.

  2. Days 3–7

    Walking and discharge

    Short walks with a walker, safe transfers to chair and toilet, and breathing exercises. Discharge is usually within 4–7 days.

  3. Week 2

    Wound check

    Stitches or staples are removed. Walking with the walker continues at home, with exercises to strengthen the hip and thigh.

  4. Weeks 2–6

    Building strength

    Walking distance increases daily. A follow-up X-ray at about 6 weeks checks that the fracture is holding in position.

  5. Weeks 6–12

    From walker to stick

    As new bone (callus) forms around the fracture, most people progress from a walker to a stick.

  6. Weeks 12–16

    Fracture united

    The fracture usually heals by 3–4 months. Most patients walk independently or with a stick outdoors.

  7. Months 6–12

    Full recovery

    Strength, balance and confidence continue to improve. Treating osteoporosis and preventing falls are essential to protect the other hip.

05

Helping your recovery at home

  • Ask for a bone density check; osteoporosis treatment greatly reduces the risk of another fracture.
  • Make the home safer: good lighting, no loose rugs, grab rails in the bathroom.
  • Keep up calcium, vitamin D and protein intake as advised.
  • Continue balance and strength exercises long after the fracture has healed.

When to contact the clinic urgently

  • Fever, or increasing redness, warmth or discharge from the wound
  • Calf pain or swelling, or sudden chest pain or breathlessness (seek emergency care)
  • New numbness, tingling, or a cold or pale limb
  • A sudden increase in pain, a new deformity, or being unable to move or bear weight as before

FOR YOUR CONSULTATION

Questions to ask
